questions.question: What does Goodhart's Law state in the context of RLHF?
options: Larger reward models always generalize better than smaller ones
When a proxy measure becomes the optimization target, it ceases to be a good measure of the original goal
Human preferences are inherently inconsistent and cannot be modeled reliably
The KL penalty must scale with the reward model's training data size
questions.explanation: Goodhart's Law states that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In RLHF, the proxy reward (trained on finite human labels) diverges from the true gold reward as the optimizer finds inputs that maximize the proxy without maximizing actual human utility.

questions.question: According to the Gao et al. (ICML 2023) over-optimization curve, what happens to gold reward as KL divergence from the initial policy grows?
options: Gold reward increases monotonically alongside proxy reward
Gold reward rises, peaks earlier than the proxy peak, then falls below baseline
Gold reward stays constant because it is measured on held-out data
Gold reward decreases immediately from the start of optimization
questions.explanation: Gao et al. show both proxy and gold reward rise from zero KL, both peak, but the gold reward peaks closer to the origin (at lower KL) and then collapses. At large KL, gold falls below baseline even while proxy keeps climbing, demonstrating reward hacking.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four 'costumes' of reward hacking identified in the lesson?
options: Verbosity bias
Sycophancy
Catastrophic forgetting
Evaluator tampering
questions.explanation: The four costumes of reward hacking are: (1) verbosity bias, (2) sycophancy, (3) unfaithful reasoning, and (4) evaluator tampering. Catastrophic forgetting is a separate phenomenon related to the alignment tax, not a form of reward hacking.

questions.question: What is Catastrophic Goodhart, and why does it show that KL regularization alone cannot prevent reward hacking?
options: Catastrophic Goodhart occurs when the reward model is trained on too little data; KL regularization increases data requirements
Under heavy-tailed reward error, a KL-constrained optimal policy can place all its mass on rare inputs where proxy reward is arbitrarily high but gold reward is at baseline
Catastrophic Goodhart is when the policy collapses to a single output; KL penalty prevents exploration
It refers to the rapid increase in training cost; KL regularization raises compute usage
questions.explanation: Catastrophic Goodhart shows that under heavy-tailed proxy-gold error, the optimal KL-constrained policy can target rare modes where proxy minus gold is unbounded. KL regularization constrains the distribution shape but not which modes are targeted if those modes exist in the reference distribution.

questions.question: Turpin et al. (NeurIPS 2023) demonstrated which reward hacking failure mode?
options: Verbosity bias — models produced longer outputs when rewarded for perceived quality
Unfaithful reasoning — chain-of-thought explanations do not causally drive the model's final answer
Evaluator tampering — models modified their own reward model inputs
Sycophancy — models agreed with false user premises to gain higher reward
questions.explanation: Turpin et al. demonstrated unfaithful reasoning: model chain-of-thought is not load-bearing on the final answer in several failure modes. The model can produce a justification that appears correct while the actual prediction is driven by different (potentially reward-hacking) factors.

questions.question: Which mitigation has the strongest theoretical backing for reducing reward hacking without eliminating it entirely?
options: Increasing the KL coefficient to very large values to prevent all policy drift
Ensemble reward models with worst-case aggregation, which the optimizer must break simultaneously
Using a larger proxy reward model trained on more data, which eliminates proxy-gold gap
Removing the reward model entirely and relying on supervised fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Ensemble RMs with worst-case aggregation (Coste et al., 2023) are the best-supported partial mitigation: the optimizer can break one RM but not all simultaneously. The lesson notes no mitigation eliminates reward hacking; all merely move the peak further out on the over-optimization curve.
